lines: The email column is supposedly masked for anyone on the analyst team, and somehow an analyst still gets the real addresses.

Three different queries ran. One filtered straight on the masked column. One hit a table built from a copy of the data. One read a file straight out of storage. Which of those did the masking actually cover, and which one slipped past it?
Here's the line that actually matters, and it's worth drawing clearly.
A filter written into the application only protects whoever's request goes through that particular application.
A policy written into the engine itself applies to every single query against that table, no matter who sends it or what tool they're using.
So try this one before I tell you.
A table holds three thousand customer rows, and there's no row-security policy on it yet. Query it as the role that's eventually going to be restricted. How many rows come back?
answer: Every single one of them. A role's name alone restricts nothing — nothing has actually told the engine to hold anything back yet.
Until a policy exists on that table, whatever grants that role holds just apply, in full.

lines: And that's exactly what happens when it's actually run.
With no policy anywhere in sight, that role's query comes back with the entire table — all three thousand rows, measured directly.
Here's what a row-security policy actually is, underneath all the vendor terminology.
It's a yes-or-no expression the engine checks against every single row, and it runs before whatever the user's own query asked for.
There's exactly one carve-out — a function proven mathematically incapable of leaking anything might get run a touch earlier by the optimizer. Everything else waits its turn.
Same test, new twist. Work it out first.
Put a policy on that table limiting this role to one region — which happens to be a third of the rows. Run the exact same query again. Nothing about the query itself changed. How many rows this time?
answer: Exactly whatever the policy allows — full stop.
The policy gets checked whether or not the query's own conditions ever mention it. The query never had to ask for anything; the engine asked on its own.

lines: And sure enough: the identical query, not touched at all, now comes back with exactly one thousand rows out of the three thousand that exist.
The policy decided that. The query had nothing to do with it.
Now look at what actually happened under the hood, not just at the row count.
Read the plan the engine chose before any policy existed, and there's no extra step in it at all. Read the plan again after the policy goes on, and a whole new step shows up — a Filter.
Whenever an engine has to choose between running fast and keeping something secret, it chooses secret, every time, even when that costs more.
One more thing worth knowing, because it closes the loop on the Hook.
A superuser account — the kind that's allowed to bypass this entire mechanism by design — still sees all three thousand rows, measured directly, policy or no policy.

Reading the underlying file straight off disk works exactly the same way. So does a copy someone already pulled out, or a view built on top that nobody thought to protect. None of those ever ask the engine anything in the first place.
So here's the whole shape of it.
A policy inside the engine runs before the query, covers every caller, and can genuinely cost something to run — all three measured directly.
None of that reaches whoever never had to go through the engine at all. That gap is exactly where the Hook's leak came from.
